claims.text: Local chemical inhomogeneities, particularly Nb/Ta-rich regions, enhance electron–phonon coupling enough to support Cooper pairing below a critical temperature.
Variations in the near-random atomic arrangement locally enhance the density of states at the Fermi level.
Localized enhancements of the density of states at the Fermi level are necessary for superconductivity in this alloy.
The proposed starting material is an approximately equimolar, disordered, defect-minimized BCC HfNbTaTiZr-like alloy.
An equimolar composition maximizes configurational disorder.
Increasing Nb and/or Ta by approximately 5–10 at.% is expected to enhance the local electron count.
Increasing Nb and/or Ta by approximately 5–10 at.% is expected to enhance electron–phonon coupling.
Local chemical inhomogeneities and their associated minute lattice distortions enhance electron–phonon coupling in specific regions.
Nb/Ta enrichment makes the proposed coupling-enhanced regions form more readily.
The coupling-enhanced regions have a higher density of electronic states conducive to superconducting pairing.
Superconductivity in the alloy is conventional and electron–phonon mediated.
Compositionally induced enhancement of electron–phonon coupling increases the superconducting pairing interaction.
Nb/Ta-rich regions can have an increased local density of states at the Fermi level, thereby promoting Cooper-pair formation below Tc.
Increasing Nb/Ta relative to the equimolar baseline should raise the superconducting transition temperature.
Increasing Nb/Ta should produce a more robust zero-resistance state and an enhanced diamagnetic response.
Reducing Nb/Ta should suppress or possibly eliminate superconductivity under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed relationship should hold below 10 K and for composition changes within approximately ±10 at.% provided the BCC phase is preserved.
Phase separation or a structural transition may invalidate the proposed composition–superconductivity relationship by altering electronic properties.
Microstructural defects, grain boundaries, and impurity phases may independently influence superconductivity.
A lack of systematic Tc increase or enhancement of zero resistance or diamagnetic screening with increasing Nb/Ta would reject the hypothesis.
